content: A bezoar, also known as an enterolith, is a type of calculus or concretion that forms as a stone within the intestines. While they are most commonly found in ruminant animals, bezoars can also occur in humans. These formations are composed of ingested foreign materials that accumulate in the gastrointestinal tract. Bezoars are classified based on their composition, which can be either organic or inorganic. The most common types are trichobezoars, which are made of hair, and phytobezoars, which consist of undigested fruit or vegetable matter. Bezoars typically form in the stomach and may pass into the small intestine, where they can occasionally cause small bowel obstruction. Risk factors for bezoar formation include inadequate chewing, diets high in fiber, and a history of gastric surgery. Historically, bezoars were highly sought after due to the belief that they possessed universal antidotal properties against poisons. It was thought that a drinking glass containing a bezoar could neutralize any poison poured into it. The term bezoar originates from the Persian word pâdzahr, meaning protection from poison. Some types of trichobezoars have been shown to bind arsenic compounds, which were historically used as poisons. In 1575, the French surgeon Ambroise Paré conducted an experiment to test the purported antidotal properties of bezoars. A cook, caught stealing silverware, agreed to be poisoned as part of the test. Despite using a bezoar, the cook died in agony, proving that bezoars could not cure all poisons as was widely believed at the time. A notable legal case in England, Chandelor v. Lopus (1603), established the principle of caveat emptor or let the buyer beware, after a purchaser sued for the return of money spent on a fraudulent bezoar. This case highlighted judicial skepticism regarding the supposed magical properties of bezoars and influenced consumer protection laws for centuries. The Merck Manual of Diagnosis and Therapy notes that persimmons have been linked to outbreaks of intestinal bezoars, with up to 90% of food boluses caused by excessive consumption of the fruit requiring surgical removal. In addition to their medical significance, bezoars have cultural and historical importance. Sacred natural gemstones, often considered bezoar stones, were first documented in Hindu texts such as the Garuda Purana and later in the Brihat-Samhita by the Indian mathematician Varahamihira. These include pearls from various sources, such as conch shells, cobras, boars, elephants, bamboo, whales, fish, and even clouds. Western documentation of bezoars and non-oyster pearls appeared in the 18th-century work Cabinet of Natural Curiosities by Albertus Seba, which showcased a collection of these items in a precursor to modern museums. Today, the original volume is on permanent display at the Koninklijke Bibliotheek in The Hague, Netherlands. Bezoars can be categorized into several types based on their composition. Food boli, which mimic true bezoars, are aggregates of food items such as seeds, fruit pits, or other materials like shellac, bubble gum, or certain medications. Pharmacobezoars, or medication bezoars, consist of tablets or semi-liquid drug masses and are often seen in patients with impaired digestion or reduced gastric motility. Trichobezoars, formed from ingested hair, are an extreme form of hairball and may require removal in individuals who compulsively consume hair. This condition is sometimes referred to as Rapunzel syndrome. Other types of bezoars include those formed from stones or sand, typically in young children, and ox bezoars, which are used in traditional Chinese medicine under the name niu-huang. In alchemy, a mineral bezoar was an emetic powder made from antimony, treated with spirit of nitre, and softened through repeated washing. This preparation was believed to promote sweating, similar to the effects attributed to bezoar stones. Bezoars have also appeared in popular culture, such as in the Harry Potter series, where they are described as stones from a goat's stomach that can protect against most poisons. In Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince, Harry uses a bezoar to save Ron Weasley's life after he accidentally consumes poisoned mead. The first mentions of bezoars in literature come from Arabic and Persian writers, with references dating back to works attributed to Aristotle and the 10th-century Persian medical text by Abu Mansur Muwaffak. A comprehensive monograph on bezoars was written in 1625 by Caspar Bauhin, a physician and professor in Basel, summarizing the knowledge of bezoars and their attributed properties at the time.
